patient.name: Zara Ahmed
patient.setting: GP surgery phlebotomy room, then the Urgent Treatment Centre
patient.complaint: Collapsed with brief loss of consciousness during a blood test
background: First-year law student at Queen Mary, lives in halls
Skipped breakfast, stood in a hot queue for 40 minutes
Fainted once before at a vaccination aged 14
No regular medication; no family history of sudden death

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young person who faints after standing, heat, pain or a needle, with a prodrome and rapid full recovery; the trap is brief jerking, which tempts you towards seizure.

points: Zara stood 40 minutes in a hot queue, no breakfast.
As the needle goes in she feels **hot, sick and lightheaded**.
Her vision narrows to a tunnel; ears ring.
She slumps from the chair to the floor.

steps.lead: A sudden drop in heart rate and BP cut Zara's brain perfusion for a few seconds: a **simple faint**.

points: Nurse sees her go **pale and sweaty**.
Both arms jerk for about 5 seconds.
Eyes open within 20 seconds; talking normally in a minute.
No tongue biting, no incontinence, **no confusion afterwards**.

steps.lead: Zara had the textbook **prodrome**, a classic **trigger** (needle, heat, standing) and a quick, complete recovery.

steps.q: Her arms jerked for 5 seconds. What makes this a faint, not a seizure?
steps.r: Brief jerks happen in faints too. The **absence of a post-ictal phase** is the key feature that separates it from a seizure.

steps.lead: Zara's jerks are just a brain briefly short of blood. She was fully herself straight away: **no post-ictal phase**.

steps.title: Faint vs seizure vs cardiac syncope
head: Feature
Vasovagal
Seizure
Cardiac (arrhythmia)

visual.title: Time to full recovery
bands: Prolonged: think seizure or other cause
visual.label: Zara 1 min
visual.caption: Recovery in seconds to a minute, with no confusion, fits a faint.

steps.lead: Zara bumped her elbow on the chair: in vasovagal syncope the real danger is **injury from the fall**.

steps.text: Fainting **during exertion**, with palpitations, chest pain, or a family history of sudden death is not a simple faint: think cardiac syncope.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (12-lead ECG, to exclude an arrhythmia) or a stem where a typical history and normal ECG mean no further tests are needed.

steps.q: Zara is fully recovered. What test should every patient with transient loss of consciousness have?
steps.r: A **12-lead ECG** to exclude an arrhythmic cause. CT and EEG are not routine for a typical faint.

steps.lead: Zara's **12-lead ECG** and basic bloods (FBC, glucose, U&E) are done at the Urgent Treatment Centre.

visual.title: Zara's 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal PR, QRS and QTc: no heart block, pre-excitation, Brugada pattern or long QT.

steps.title: Basic bloods
steps.text: Nothing to suggest anaemia, hypoglycaemia or an electrolyte cause.

steps.lead: With a classic story and a normal ECG, Zara's diagnosis is **clinical**. No further tests are needed.

steps.title: Blackout: what to look for on the ECG
steps.caption: The ECG is there to catch dangerous causes.

steps.text: Do not send a typical faint for **EEG** or **CT head** because of a few jerks. Investigate only when the story is atypical.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next step?' where the answer is reassurance and discharge with trigger advice, or 'lie down and raise the legs' for a prodrome.

steps.q: Zara starts to feel hot and sick again when she sits up. What should she do?
o: Lie down and raise her legs
Sit with her head between her knees
steps.r: **Lie flat and elevate the legs** to restore cerebral perfusion and stop the faint.

steps.lead: The nurse lies Zara flat with her **legs raised** on a chair, and the prodrome settles within a minute.

visual.title: Zara's observations
visual.caption: Sudden fall in both heart rate and BP, then quick recovery once flat with legs raised.

steps.lead: Zara is **reassured** that this is benign and advised to **stay hydrated**, eat beforehand, avoid long standing and overheating, and to lie down for blood tests.
Zara needs **no medication**: uncomplicated vasovagal syncope is managed with advice alone.

steps.title: Plan for Zara
nodes: Teach: lie down, legs up at the first warning
Avoid triggers; fluids and regular meals

steps.lead: **NICE CG109**: a typical vasovagal faint with a normal ECG needs no further assessment; explain the diagnosis and discharge.

steps.text: A simple faint with a clear trigger and prodrome does **not** stop someone driving under DVLA rules.

science.exam: Expect 'Which is the mechanism of a vasovagal attack?' (reflex vagal bradycardia plus vasodilation) and applied questions on why legs up helps or why jerks do not mean epilepsy.

steps.lead: The needle and the heat set off an **exaggerated vagal reflex** in Zara: her heart slowed and her vessels dilated together.

steps.title: The reflex
nodes: Low cardiac output and SVR: BP falls

steps.lead: Zara's HR fell to 46 and her vessels opened, so BP fell until her brain dropped below the perfusion needed to stay conscious.

steps.q: Why did raising Zara's legs help?
steps.r: Raising the legs increases **venous return**, restoring cardiac output and cerebral perfusion.

steps.lead: Gravity sends blood pooled in Zara's legs back to her heart, so cardiac output and brain perfusion recover and the episode ends.
Zara's jerks came from **brief cerebral hypoperfusion**, not an electrical storm, so there was nothing to recover from afterwards.

steps.text: BP = cardiac output x SVR. A faint drops **both** (bradycardia and vasodilation), which is why BP falls so fast.

glossary.Syncope: Transient loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain, with spontaneous full recovery.
glossary.Vasovagal: Involving the vagus nerve and blood vessels: slowing of the heart plus vessel dilation.
glossary.Reflex syncope: Fainting caused by an inappropriate autonomic reflex; vasovagal is the commonest type.
glossary.Prodrome: Warning symptoms just before an event, such as feeling hot, sick and lightheaded before a faint.
glossary.Tunnel vision: Loss of peripheral vision so only the centre remains, a common pre-faint symptom.
glossary.TLoC: Transient loss of consciousness: the umbrella term NICE uses for blackouts.
glossary.Post-ictal: The period of confusion, drowsiness and headache after a seizure; absent after a faint.
glossary.Convulsions: Involuntary jerking movements; brief ones can occur in faints as well as seizures.
glossary.Myoclonic jerks: Brief, shock-like muscle twitches; in faints caused by cerebral hypoperfusion.
glossary.Cerebral perfusion: Blood flow to the brain; consciousness is lost when it falls too low.
glossary.Vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, which lowers vascular resistance and blood pressure.
glossary.Parasympathetic: The rest-and-digest part of the autonomic nervous system, carried largely by the vagus nerve.
glossary.Sympathetic withdrawal: Sudden loss of sympathetic tone to vessels, letting them dilate.
glossary.SVR: Systemic vascular resistance: the resistance to flow across the body's circulation.
glossary.Cardiac output: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume: blood pumped per minute.
glossary.Venous return: Blood flow back to the heart; raising the legs increases it.
glossary.Venous pooling: Blood collecting in the leg veins on standing, reducing return to the heart.
glossary.12-lead ECG: A standard recording of the heart's electrical activity from 12 views; first-line after any blackout.
glossary.QTc: QT interval corrected for heart rate; a long QTc risks dangerous arrhythmias.
glossary.Brugada: An inherited sodium channel disorder with a coved ST pattern in V1–V2 and risk of sudden death.
glossary.Delta wave: A slurred QRS upstroke showing an accessory pathway, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White.
glossary.HOCM: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, a cause of syncope on exertion.
glossary.Orthostatic hypotension: A fall in BP of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.
glossary.Tilt-table test: A test tilting the patient upright to provoke reflex syncope; reserved for unclear recurrent cases.
glossary.EEG: Electroencephalogram: recording of brain electrical activity, used for suspected epilepsy.
glossary.Venepuncture: Taking blood from a vein, a classic vasovagal trigger.
glossary.Fludrocortisone: A mineralocorticoid that expands plasma volume; not needed for uncomplicated faints.
glossary.Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: Syncope from pressure on the neck (shaving, tight collar), usually in older people.
glossary.DVLA: UK driving licensing agency; a simple faint with a clear trigger needs no driving restriction.

technique.stem: A 22 year old man collapses while standing in a crowded, hot underground train. Before collapsing he felt warm, nauseated and his vision went grey. A passenger saw him go pale and his arms twitch for a few seconds. He came round within 30 seconds and was fully orientated straight away.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis for a transient loss of consciousness: faint, fit or heart?

clues: standing in a crowded, hot underground train
felt warm, nauseated and his vision went grey
arms twitch for a few seconds
steps.x: Classic triggers, a prodrome, brief jerks and no post-ictal phase.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Vasovagal syncope**.

elim: Arrhythmias usually have no prodrome and may follow exertion or palpitations.
A seizure would leave him confused afterwards.
Hypoglycaemia does not recover in 30 seconds without treatment.
Orthostatic hypotension follows getting up, often in older people on drugs.

steps.x: **E. Vasovagal syncope.** Trigger + prodrome + rapid full recovery.

technique.stem: A 17 year old girl faints in assembly after standing for 30 minutes. She felt hot and sick beforehand and recovered fully within a minute. She has no palpitations or chest pain, and no family history of sudden death. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg lying and standing.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation in a blackout.

clues: no family history of sudden death
steps.x: A typical faint with no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Everyone with a blackout gets a **12-lead ECG** to exclude an arrhythmia.

elim: Ambulatory ECG is for suspected arrhythmia with an abnormal ECG or palpitations.
CT head is not needed: no head injury or focal signs.
EEG is for suspected epilepsy.
Tilt-table testing is for unclear recurrent episodes.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** If normal with a typical story, no more tests.

technique.stem: A 25 year old woman has had two faints in a year, both while queuing on hot days. Each time she felt warm, sweaty and lightheaded first, and recovered fully within a minute. Her ECG is normal. She asks what she should do if the warning symptoms start again.

o: Lie down and raise her legs

steps.x: Advice for the prodrome.
Recurrent vasovagal syncope with a clear prodrome.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lie down and elevate the legs**.

elim: Paper-bag breathing is not advised, even for hyperventilation.
This is not hypoglycaemia.
Staying upright lets the faint happen.
No drug treatment is needed.

steps.x: **C. Lie down and raise her legs.** Restores cerebral perfusion and stops LOC.

technique.stem: A 20 year old man feels faint while giving blood. His pulse rate falls from 84 to 44 bpm and his BP from 118/72 to 76/40 mmHg. He is laid flat and his legs are raised on pillows. Within 2 minutes he feels better and his BP is 106/64 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which raising his legs helped?
o: Increased venous return to the heart

steps.x: A mechanism question about the treatment.
Vasovagal bradycardia and hypotension, corrected by legs up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gravity increases **venous return**, raising cardiac output and cerebral perfusion.

elim: Position does not directly switch off vagal tone.
Intracranial pressure is not the problem.
Brain oxygen demand does not change.
No adrenaline surge is needed for this effect.

steps.x: **B. Increased venous return.** More preload, more output, more brain perfusion.

felt sick and hot and her vision blurred

practice.stem: A 16 year old boy faints in church after standing for an hour. Witnesses say he went pale and his arms and legs jerked for about 5 seconds. He came round within a minute. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. His mother wants to know if he has epilepsy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No post-ictal phase**: rapid full recovery.

elim: Brief jerks happen in both faints and seizures.
Cyanosis favours a tonic-clonic seizure.
Lateral tongue biting favours a seizure.

practice.stem: A 19 year old soldier collapses during a long parade on a hot day after standing to attention for 2 hours. He felt hot, lightheaded and nauseated beforehand. practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Prolonged standing in heat with a prodrome and quick recovery is classic vasovagal syncope. Heat stroke would have a high temperature and confusion.

elim: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is in older people with neck pressure.

steps.x: **E. Vasovagal syncope.** Prolonged standing in the heat is the textbook trigger.
